newsitem.title: CANADA: RCMP form special Busang squad, broker faces suit.
newsitem.headline: RCMP form special Busang squad, broker faces suit.

text.p: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police formed a special fraud squad to probe the Bre-X Minerals scandal on Friday, while shareholders took aim at Canada's financial community for the first time with a class action lawsuit against a major brokerage.
The RCMP said 10 officers from across Canada have been assigned to the investigation, which fraud experts predict will be long and complicated.
"At this time the team members are proceeding with the investigation, making initial inquiries both within Canada and in Indonesia," Canada's national police said in a statement.
In Jakarta, an RCMP liaison officer held talks with Indonesian police on the Busang affair on Friday, but no details were released.

The RCMP earlier this week received two separate fraud complaints from Bre-X Chief Executive David Walsh and the Ontario Securities Commission, Canada's top securities regulator. The Ontario Securities Commission also is conducting its own probe.
As police delve deeper into the case, a group of Bre-X shareholders filed a class action suit against Toronto-based brokerage Nesbitt Burns Inc., a unit of Bank of Montreal.

The suit, filed by a Windsor, Ontario law firm, is the first court action against a major Canadian broker involved in the Bre-X saga. Canada's financial community has come under fire for failing to spot the massive fraud which cost investors millions of dollars.
Nesbitt Burns declined to comment.
Bre-X already faces at least nine class actions lawsuits filed in Canada and the United States.
Meanwhile, Canadian police said a lawyer in the Vancouver, British Columbia-area who committed suicide last month probably was despondent over big losses from a Bre-X investment.

Lawrence Beadle, 62, shot himself to death on April 7, several days after Bre-X shares sank 80 percent on a negative report from Busang partner Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. The Vancouver Sun newspaper reported that his losses were around C$3 million ($2.2 million).

Embattled Bre-X filed for creditor protection on Thursday after a consultant's report late Sunday concluded Busang was falsified and the site once touted as the gold find of the century contained no gold worth mining.
Director Rolando Francisco quit Bre-X's board on Friday. following the resignations of two directors this week.
Bre-X was delisted on the Toronto and Nasdaq stock exchanges this week after the stock -- once worth more than C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) -- sank to pennies a share.
Bre-X's ousted exploration chief John Felderhof, who is now in the Cayman Islands, said on Friday he was unaware of any fraud at Busang and had not lost faith in his work there.
In a statement released through his lawyers in Toronto and Houston, Felderhof said he has reviewing the "startling new material" on Busang, but added more facts were needed.
"Again, let me state without reservation that I was not aware of any fraud at Busang, Loa Duri, or Bre-X," said Felderhof, who was fired by Bre-X on Thursday.
Published reports have suggested salting, an industry term for tampering, occurred at a warehouse in the riverside hamlet of Loa Duri.

Indonesian Trade Minister Tunky Ariwibowo said the Bre-X affair will not hurt trade ties between Canada and Indonesia. "It happened not on the Indonesian side, but on the Canadian side. I see from the media that it is a corporate problem really," he told reporters during a trade ministers' meeting in Montreal.
The scandal over the worthless gold find is making it tougher for other small Canadian mining firms to raise funds.
After losing millions of dollars on the Busang gold bust, fund managers are pressuring other companies for more details of their far-flung projects.
"It's ridiculous. Everyone is panicking," said an official with one Toronto-based exploration company on Friday.

The Busang gold scandal will likely scare off investors from smaller mining companies in the near term, investment advisors said. But they predicted a healthier mining sector will emerge after Bre-X has faded into history.

"Investor appetite for junior exploration companies I would say has largely come to an end," Barry Allan, an analyst with Toronto-based Gordon Capital Corp., told a mining finance conference in Toronto.
